L1.1.title: Hardware and the Input-Process-Output Cycle
L1.1.concept: A computer system takes data in, works on it, and sends results out. That pattern is the input-process-output cycle, and storage keeps data or programs for later use. Input devices collect data from the user or the environment, such as a keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone or sensor. The processor, usually the central processing unit (CPU), carries out the instructions of a stored program. Inside the CPU, the arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) performs calculations and comparisons, and the control unit directs the other parts so that instructions are fetched from memory and executed in order. Main memory holds the programs and data that are in use. Random-access memory (RAM) is volatile: its contents are lost when the power goes off. Read-only memory (ROM) is non-volatile and keeps the start-up instructions. Secondary storage, such as a solid-state drive or hard disk, keeps files after the computer is switched off. A bus is the pathway that carries data and control signals between these components. HKDSE questions ask you to name the stage or the device, not to describe chip design.

example.scenario: A school attendance kiosk reads a student card, checks the record, shows "Present" on the screen, and writes the time into a file on the drive.
example.walkthrough: Reading the card is input. Checking the record against the stored list is processing, done by the CPU using data held in RAM. Showing "Present" is output. Writing the time into a file is storage on secondary storage, so the record is still there after a restart. If the program only kept the record in RAM, a power cut would wipe it.

traps: Calling the screen an input device. A display is output; a keyboard, scanner or sensor is input.
Saying RAM keeps files after shutdown. RAM is volatile; secondary storage is not.
Describing the control unit as the part that does the arithmetic. Arithmetic and comparisons belong to the ALU.

terms.definition: The pattern of entering data, working on it, and producing a result, with storage used to keep data for later.
The processor that fetches and executes program instructions.
The part of the CPU that performs arithmetic and logical comparisons.
Volatile main memory used for programs and data that are currently in use.
Non-volatile storage, such as an SSD, that keeps files when the power is off.

L1.2.title: System Software and Application Software
L1.2.concept: Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. System software manages the computer itself. The operating system is the main piece of system software: it controls hardware, organises files, manages memory, and lets the user start applications. Utility software does a housekeeping job, such as virus scanning, file compression, disk checking or backup. Device drivers let the operating system talk to a particular printer, camera or network card. Application software helps the user do a task: a browser, a spreadsheet, a photo editor or a school learning platform. An application cannot replace the operating system. If the operating system fails to start, the applications stored on the disk cannot run, even though the files are still there. In an exam, classify the named program before you explain it. "Word processor" is an application. "Operating system" and "backup utility" are system software. Do not treat a brand name as a category unless the question asks for an example.

example.scenario: A notebook in the ICT room will not reach the desktop after a failed system update. The word-processor files are still on the SSD, but they cannot be opened.
example.walkthrough: The operating system is system software that must load before applications can run. The word processor is application software. The files on the SSD are data in secondary storage, not the operating system itself. Reinstalling or repairing the operating system is the relevant fix. Buying another word processor does not start a machine whose operating system will not load. A backup utility would matter later, when restoring the files, but it is not what displays the desktop.

traps: Calling a browser or spreadsheet system software. They are applications that rely on the operating system.
Saying a driver is an application for editing photos. A driver is system software that links a device to the operating system.
Assuming a file on the SSD can be opened with no operating system running.

terms.definition: System software that manages hardware, files and memory, and provides a way to run applications.
System software that performs a maintenance task such as scanning, compression or backup.
Software that helps a user carry out a task, such as writing, calculating or browsing.
Software that lets the operating system communicate with a specific hardware device.

L1.3.title: Input, Output and Storage Devices
L1.3.concept: Choosing a device means matching it to the job. Input devices capture data: a keyboard for text, a barcode scanner for stock codes, a microphone for sound, a sensor for temperature. Output devices present results: a monitor, a printer, a speaker, a projector. Some devices do both, such as a touchscreen, which displays output and accepts touch as input. Storage devices keep data. A solid-state drive has no spinning disk, so it is usually faster and more shock-resistant than a hard disk, but both are secondary storage. A USB flash drive is portable secondary storage, not main memory. Capacity, speed and portability are the usual comparison points. A school should also think about who needs access: a shared network folder is not a device, but the file server that holds it is a computer providing storage to others. When a question lists four devices, cross out the ones that perform the wrong stage of the cycle. A printer cannot capture a photo. A scanner cannot display a slide to the class.

example.scenario: The drama club wants to record a rehearsal, edit the clip, show it on the hall screen, and keep a copy for next year.
example.walkthrough: A camera or microphone captures the rehearsal, so that is input. Editing is processing in an application, using RAM while the work is open. The projector or hall display is output. Saving the finished file to the school's shared drive, or to an external SSD kept by the teacher, is secondary storage. Showing the clip only from RAM would lose it when the editing computer is turned off. A speaker is output for sound, not a place to store the video file.

traps: Treating a touchscreen as output only. It is both an output display and an input device.
Calling a USB flash drive RAM. It is portable secondary storage.
Choosing a printer when the question asks for a device that captures an image.

terms.definition: Hardware that captures data for the computer, such as a keyboard, scanner or sensor.
Hardware that presents results, such as a monitor, printer, speaker or projector.
Secondary storage with no spinning disk, used to keep files when the power is off.
A device that both displays output and accepts input by touch.

L2.1.title: Number Systems and Units of Data
L2.1.concept: Computers store everything as bits. A bit is a binary digit, 0 or 1. Eight bits make one byte. Binary is base 2, denary is base 10, and hexadecimal is base 16. Hexadecimal uses the digits 0-9 and the letters A-F, where A is 10 and F is 15. Two hexadecimal digits represent one byte, because 16 times 16 is 256, the same number of patterns as eight bits. To convert binary to denary, add the place values that contain a 1. For example, 1101 is 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. To convert denary to binary, find the largest power of two that fits and repeat. In these lessons, 1 KB = 1024 bytes and 1 MB = 1024 KB, which is the convention used in HKDSE data-size calculations unless a question says otherwise. Do not mix bits and bytes: divide by 8 when you change bits into bytes. Show the unit in the answer. A question that asks for bytes is wrong if you stop at bits, even when the number itself is calculated correctly.

example.scenario: A colour code is written as the hexadecimal value 2F. A student says this is the same as the denary number 215.
example.walkthrough: 2F in hexadecimal is 2 times 16, plus F. F is 15, so 32 + 15 = 47 in denary, not 215. In binary, 47 is 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1, which is 101111. As a byte it is written 00101111. The student treated the letter F as a denary digit and also misread the place values. Two hex digits are exactly one byte, so 2F is one byte, not two.

traps: Treating a hexadecimal letter as a denary digit. A to F mean 10 to 15.
Forgetting to divide by 8 when the working is in bits but the answer must be in bytes.
Using 1 KB = 1000 bytes in a question that expects the 1024-byte convention, or the reverse, without reading the question.

terms.definition: A single binary digit, either 0 or 1.
A group of 8 bits.
Base 16, using digits 0-9 and letters A-F. Two hex digits represent one byte.
In these drills, 1024 bytes, unless a question states a different convention.

L2.2.title: Text, Images and Character Codes
L2.2.concept: Text is stored as numeric codes. ASCII uses one byte for each character and covers English letters, digits and common symbols, so it cannot represent the full range of Chinese characters. Unicode is a much larger coding system designed so that characters from many languages, including Chinese, can be stored. A character code is not the same as a font: the code identifies the character, and the font decides how it looks on screen. Images are stored in two main ways. A bitmap is a grid of pixels. Its uncompressed size depends on the width in pixels, the height in pixels, and the colour depth, which is the number of bits used for each pixel. The number of possible colours is 2 to the power of the colour depth: 1 bit gives 2 colours, 8 bits give 256 colours. Uncompressed bitmap size in bytes is width times height times colour depth, divided by 8. A vector image stores shapes as instructions, such as lines and curves, so it can be enlarged without becoming blocky. A photograph of a sports day is a bitmap; a school logo made of simple shapes is a good candidate for a vector.

example.scenario: An uncompressed bitmap is 100 pixels wide and 80 pixels tall, with a colour depth of 4 bits. Find the file size in bytes.
example.walkthrough: Each pixel uses 4 bits, and there are 100 times 80 = 8000 pixels. Total bits = 8000 times 4 = 32000. Bytes = 32000 divided by 8 = 4000 bytes. Colour depth of 4 bits means 16 possible colours, not 4 colours. Do not multiply by 4 again after you have already used the colour depth, and do not forget to divide by 8 if the question asks for bytes.

traps: Saying an 8-bit image has 8 colours. It has 2 to the power 8, which is 256 colours.
Leaving the file size in bits when the question asks for bytes.
Claiming ASCII can store every Chinese character. It cannot; Unicode is the coding system built for many languages.

terms.definition: The number of bits used to store the colour of one pixel.
An image stored as a grid of pixels.
An image stored as geometric instructions, which stays sharp when enlarged.
A character coding system that can represent characters from many writing systems, including Chinese.

L2.3.title: Sound Representation
L2.3.concept: Sound is analogue in the air, but a computer stores it as numbers. Sampling measures the sound wave at regular intervals. The sampling rate is how many samples are taken each second, in hertz. A higher sampling rate records higher frequencies more faithfully and increases the file size. The sample size, or bit depth, is how many bits store each sample. More bits mean finer differences in loudness and a larger file. A mono recording has one channel. Stereo has two, so the uncompressed file is about twice the size of the same mono recording. Uncompressed size in bytes is sampling rate times sample size in bits times the number of channels times the duration in seconds, divided by 8. Compression such as MP3 reduces the file size by discarding some detail; that is lossy compression. A WAV file is commonly used for uncompressed audio, so it is larger. For a school podcast that must stay small enough to download on a phone, a compressed format is the practical choice. For editing the original recording, keep a less compressed master.

example.scenario: A 5-second mono clip is sampled at 8000 Hz with an 8-bit sample size, and it is not compressed. A student estimates the file at 320000 bytes.
example.walkthrough: Size in bytes = 8000 times 8 times 1 channel times 5 seconds, divided by 8. The two 8s cancel, leaving 8000 times 5 = 40000 bytes. The student forgot to divide by 8 and reported the number of bits. Stereo would double the result to 80000 bytes. Raising the sampling rate or the sample size would also increase the size. Compression could make the stored file smaller than this uncompressed figure, but the question says the clip is not compressed.

traps: Reporting bits as if they were bytes.
Forgetting the channel count, so a stereo file is treated as the same size as mono.
Saying a higher sampling rate makes the file smaller. It captures more samples, so the uncompressed file is larger.

terms.definition: The number of times the sound wave is measured each second.
The number of bits used to store each sample.
A recording with one channel.
A recording with two channels, which roughly doubles the uncompressed file size.

L3.1.title: LANs, WANs and Network Devices
L3.1.concept: A network joins computers so they can share files, printers and an Internet connection. A local area network (LAN) covers a small site such as a home, a classroom or a school campus. A wide area network (WAN) joins sites across a city, a country or the world. The Internet is a WAN made of many networks. A network interface card, or the wireless adapter built into a notebook, connects a device to the network. A switch joins devices inside a LAN and forwards data to the device that needs it. A hub, an older device, repeats data to every port, so it wastes bandwidth. A router joins different networks and uses IP addresses to forward data toward its destination. A modem connects a home or school network to the line provided by an Internet service provider, by converting signals for that line. Wireless access points let devices join the LAN by Wi-Fi. In a question, decide whether the device works inside one LAN or between networks. A switch does not choose a route across the Internet. A router is not required to connect two computers that already sit on the same switch, though a home "router" box often combines several of these jobs.

example.scenario: The ICT room has 30 computers that must share one printer and reach the Internet. The computers are in one room.
example.walkthrough: The room is a LAN. A switch connects the computers and the printer's connection inside that LAN. A router joins this LAN to other networks, including the path to the Internet. A modem, or the ISP connection device the school already uses, links the site to the service provider. Putting only a hub in place would still connect the room, but every transmission would be repeated to all ports. A WAN is the wrong label for a single room.

traps: Calling the school LAN a WAN because students open websites. The campus network is still a LAN; the Internet beyond it is a WAN.
Saying a switch routes packets between different IP networks. That is the router's job.
Confusing a modem with a switch. A modem links the local network to the ISP line.

terms.definition: A network that covers a small area, such as a room, a home or a school.
A network that covers a large geographical area. The Internet is a WAN.
A device that connects devices in a LAN and forwards data to the intended device.
A device that forwards data between different networks using IP addresses.

L3.2.title: Topologies, Media and Sharing Models
L3.2.concept: A topology is the layout of a network. In a star, each device has its own cable or wireless link to a central switch. If one cable fails, only that device is cut off. If the central switch fails, the whole star stops. A bus uses one shared backbone; a break in that backbone can stop many devices, which is why new school LANs are built as stars. Transmission media carry the signals. Twisted-pair copper cable is common inside buildings. Fibre-optic cable uses light, offers high bandwidth and is less affected by electrical interference, so it suits links between buildings. Wi-Fi avoids new cables but can be slowed by walls and distance, and it needs wireless security. Sharing can be organised as client-server or peer-to-peer. In client-server, a dedicated server provides files, printing or accounts, which is easier to back up and control in a school. In peer-to-peer, each computer can share directly. That is simpler for a few home machines, but security and backups are harder because there is no single place in charge. An IP address identifies a device on a network. It is not the same as a person's name or a website's title.

example.scenario: Two campus buildings need a reliable link for a shared file server. Inside each building, a broken wall cable should not take down every computer. Students also bring phones.
example.walkthrough: A star inside each building, with a switch in the cabinet, limits a cable fault to one device. Fibre between the buildings gives a high-capacity link that is resistant to electrical noise. Wi-Fi access points let phones join, with a password so outsiders cannot use the network. A client-server file server lets the school back up one store of work. A bus between every computer would make a single cable break much more serious. Peer-to-peer sharing of the only copy of exam files would be a weak backup plan.

traps: Saying a star has no single point of failure. The central switch is a single point of failure.
Claiming fibre is used because it is always cheaper than copper. Its advantages are bandwidth and resistance to interference.
Describing peer-to-peer as the model with a dedicated file server. That is client-server.

terms.definition: A layout in which each device connects to a central switch.
A medium that transmits data as light, with high bandwidth and low electrical interference.
A model in which a dedicated server provides services to client computers.
A model in which computers share directly, with no dedicated server.

L4.1.title: The Internet, the Web and URLs
L4.1.concept: The Internet is the global network of networks. The World Wide Web is one service that runs on the Internet: documents linked by hyperlinks and requested with HTTP or HTTPS. Email, file transfer and video calls also use the Internet, but they are not the Web. A web browser displays pages. A search engine indexes pages so you can look for them; you can use a browser without a search engine by typing an address. A uniform resource locator (URL) identifies a resource. In https://www.example.edu.hk/ict/notes.html, https is the protocol, www.example.edu.hk is the host name, and /ict/notes.html is the path. HTTPS means the HTTP traffic is encrypted on the way between the browser and the site. A domain name is a human-readable name. An IP address is the numeric address of a device. The Domain Name System (DNS) translates the domain name into an IP address so the request can be delivered. An Internet service provider supplies the connection. Uploading sends data from your device to a server. Downloading brings data from a server to your device.

example.scenario: A student types https://www.hkeaa.edu.hk into a browser to read a page about ICT, and says, "I am on the Internet, so this program is a search engine."
example.walkthrough: The student is using the Internet, and the page is part of the World Wide Web because it is fetched with HTTPS. The program that displays the page is a browser, not a search engine. No search was required, because the URL was typed in full. https shows that the page request is encrypted in transit. DNS will have translated the domain name into an IP address in the background. Emailing a friend would also use the Internet, but that message would not be a web page.

traps: Treating the Internet and the World Wide Web as the same thing.
Calling the browser a search engine whenever it shows a page.
Saying HTTPS means the website's content must be true. It only encrypts the connection.

terms.definition: The global network of networks.
A service on the Internet that provides linked pages through HTTP or HTTPS.
The address of a resource, including a protocol, a host name and usually a path.
The system that translates a domain name into an IP address.

L4.2.title: Internet Services and Cloud Use
L4.2.concept: Common Internet services do different jobs. The Web shares pages. Email sends messages; at name level, SMTP is used to send mail and POP or IMAP to collect it. You do not need port numbers for the compulsory course. Streaming delivers audio or video as you watch, instead of waiting for a complete download first. A search engine helps you find pages, but the pages it lists are not automatically reliable: check the author, the date and whether other trustworthy sources agree. Cloud computing means applications or files are stored on remote servers and used over the Internet. A browser-based document editor and a school drive that you can open from home are everyday examples. The gain is access from more than one device, and the school can look after backups. The limits are a working connection, and trust: the provider holds the data, so the account needs a strong password and the school should know what personal data is stored. Uploading homework to the school cloud is not the same as publishing it on the public Web. A private shared folder still needs correct permissions so the whole Internet cannot read it.

example.scenario: The class keeps a group report in an online drive. One student can edit from home, but the file will not open on the bus when the phone has no signal. Another student worries the file is now a public web page.
example.walkthrough: The online drive is cloud storage: the file sits on a remote server and is reached over the Internet, which is why the home computer can open it and why the bus, with no connection, cannot. It is not automatically a public web page. If the sharing setting is limited to the class account, other people on the Web do not get the file. The service still holds a copy, so the login should be protected and the group should know who else has access. Streaming a video would be a different service: playback as the data arrives, not a shared editable document.

traps: Saying cloud storage works with no network connection.
Assuming every file placed on a server is published to the public Web.
Confusing a search engine's list of links with a guarantee that those pages are accurate.

terms.definition: Files kept on a remote server and opened over the Internet.
Playing audio or video while it is still being delivered, rather than after a full download.
A protocol used to send email.
A service that indexes web pages so users can search for them.

L4.3.title: Elementary Web Pages
L4.3.concept: A web page is a file that a browser displays. Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) marks the structure: this part is a heading, this part is a paragraph, this part is a link. The browser uses those marks to lay out the page. A hyperlink points at another URL, so the reader can move from one page to another without typing the address. The address in the link must be correct; a broken link is a path or file-name error, not a fault in the Internet itself. Images and other media are separate files that the page refers to. If the image file is missing or huge, the page loads slowly or shows a broken picture. Text alternatives for images help a reader who cannot see the picture, and they are part of making a page usable. Elementary authoring is about clear structure, working links, suitable file sizes and an audience. It is not a course in web frameworks. Cascading Style Sheets can control colour and layout separately from the wording, but the compulsory idea is that content and presentation can be separated. Check the page in a browser, including the links, before you treat it as finished.

example.scenario: A club page should show the club name as a heading, a short paragraph, a photo of the booth, and a link to the school homepage. On the test computer the photo icon is broken and the link opens the wrong folder.
example.walkthrough: The heading and paragraph are HTML structure. The photo is a separate image file, so a wrong file name or folder in the page will produce a broken image even when the words are correct. The link is a hyperlink whose URL points at the wrong path; edit that URL so it targets the school homepage. Compressing a very large photo, or exporting a reasonably sized JPEG or PNG, keeps the page usable on the school Wi-Fi. Adding alternative text tells non-visual users what the booth photo shows. None of this requires a new Internet connection if the files are already on the machine; the browser can open a local page.

traps: Saying HTML is a programming language that calculates results. At this level it marks up structure.
Blaming the ISP for a broken image caused by a wrong file name.
Publishing a page with no text alternative and claiming every user can use it.

terms.definition: The markup language that describes the structure of a web page.
A link that points to another URL so the reader can open that resource.
The application that requests a page and displays it.
Text that describes an image for users and tools that do not display the picture.

L5.1.title: Tables, Keys and Relationships
L5.1.concept: A database stores organised data so it can be searched and updated without keeping many conflicting copies. A table holds one kind of thing, such as students. A record is one row, one student. A field is one column, such as the class. Each field has a data type: text, number, date or yes/no. The primary key is the field, or combination of fields, chosen to identify each record. Its value must be unique and it must not be left empty. A name is a poor primary key when two students can share it. A student number that the school issues once is a better key. A foreign key is a field in one table that stores the primary key of a record in another table, so the tables can be related. In a one-to-many relationship, one class has many students, so the class code is stored on each student record. You should not be able to record a student in a class code that does not exist. That rule is referential integrity. This is school-level database work for the Databases elective, not a university course in relational theory. Design the tables on paper before you type any data.

example.scenario: The library keeps borrowers and loans. One borrower can borrow many books. BorrowerID identifies a borrower. A loan row stores LoanID, BorrowerID, BookID and the date.
example.walkthrough: BorrowerID is the primary key of the borrower table because each borrower has one unique number. In the loan table, LoanID is the primary key of that loan. BorrowerID in the loan table is a foreign key pointing at the borrower. The relationship is one-to-many: one borrower, many loans. Using the borrower's name as the primary key would fail when two people share a name, and a blank BorrowerID could not identify anyone. A loan whose BorrowerID matches no borrower breaks referential integrity and should be rejected.

traps: Using a name as the primary key when duplicates are possible.
Calling every key a primary key. A foreign key refers to another table's primary key.
Storing the same borrower's address again on every loan row when it already lives in the borrower table.

terms.definition: One row in a table, representing one person, object or event.
One column in a table, holding one item of data about each record.
The field or fields that uniquely identify each record and must not be empty.
A field that stores the primary key of a related record in another table.

L5.2.title: Queries, Forms and Reports
L5.2.concept: A query asks a question of the data. It selects records that meet criteria, can sort them, and can show only the fields you need. "Class equals 4A" is a criterion. "Name in ascending order" is a sort. A calculated field can derive a value, such as a fine of one dollar per late day, from data already stored. You do not need to memorise a large query language for these lessons: be able to say which field is tested, what the criterion is, and which fields should appear. A form is a screen layout for entering or editing one record, with labels and boxes, so the user does not type into a raw grid. A report is a formatted presentation of results, often for printing or handing to a teacher, with headings and totals. A form is for input. A report is for output. A query decides which records the form or report is based on. If the criterion is wrong, the report can be beautifully formatted and still show the wrong students. Always test a query with a small set of records whose correct answer you already know.

example.scenario: The librarian wants a printed list of overdue loans, sorted by due date, showing the borrower name and the book title, and a screen where staff can add a new loan.
example.walkthrough: The overdue list is a report. A query supplies it: the criterion is that the returned date is empty and the due date is before today, sorted by due date. Borrower name and book title come from the related tables through the keys, so the report does not need a second copy of those names typed into the loan table. The screen for adding a loan is a form. It should ask for the book and the borrower and reject a borrower number that is not in the borrower table. Printing the data-entry form is not a substitute for the overdue report.

traps: Calling a printed overdue list a form. A form is for entering or editing data.
Sorting the records and thinking that replaces a criterion. Sort order does not filter.
Typing the same name into every related table instead of linking tables with a key.

terms.definition: A question that selects, sorts or calculates data from one or more tables.
The condition a record must meet to be included, such as Class = 4A.
A screen layout used to enter or edit records.
A formatted output of records, often printed, with headings and totals.

L5.3.title: Validation, Verification and Integrity
L5.3.concept: Validation is a check that data is reasonable in form: the right type, a value inside a range, a required field that is not blank, a length limit, or a pattern such as a date. A range check on a mark from 0 to 100 rejects 150 and rejects -3. It still accepts 70 when the student actually scored 60, because 70 is inside the range. Validation does not prove that the data is true. Verification checks that data has been copied accurately, for example by typing a value twice or by proofreading the screen against the paper form. A check digit, as on a Hong Kong identity card number, catches many typing errors; it is a validation technique, not a guarantee that the person is who they claim to be. Referential integrity stops a foreign key from pointing at a missing record. Presence, type, range, length and format checks answer different threats. Use a date field for a birthday, not text, so impossible dates can be rejected and dates can be sorted properly. In an exam, name the check and say what error it catches and what error it misses.

example.scenario: A mark-entry form accepts marks from 0 to 100, requires a student number, and asks the clerk to type each mark twice. A clerk enters 72 twice for a student who scored 27. The system saves 72.
example.walkthrough: The range check is validation and 72 is allowed, so it does not catch the swapped digits. Typing the value twice is verification, but both entries match, so the swap is still missed. Proofreading against the original script would be the check that could catch it. A type check would matter if the clerk typed a letter. A presence check would matter if the student number were blank. None of these checks knows the student's real mark unless it is compared with a trusted source. The saved 72 is valid and verified as consistently typed, but it is still wrong.

traps: Saying a range check proves the mark is correct.
Confusing validation with verification. Validation tests whether the data is sensible; verification tests whether it was transcribed accurately.
Using a text field for marks and then expecting the database to reject 150.

terms.definition: An automatic check that data is reasonable, such as type, range, presence, length or format.
A check that data has been entered or copied accurately, such as double entry or proofreading.
A validation rule that accepts only values between a lower and an upper limit.
A rule that a foreign key must match an existing primary key.

L6.1.title: Multimedia Elements and File Formats
L6.1.concept: A multimedia product combines media such as text, graphics, audio, video and animation for a purpose and an audience. The file format follows the job. JPEG is a lossy format commonly used for photographs: it makes smaller files by discarding some detail, and it is a poor choice when you need sharp text or a transparent background. PNG is lossless and supports transparency, so it suits logos and screenshots. GIF is limited to 256 colours and can carry a simple animation. A vector format suits logos and diagrams that must be enlarged. For sound, MP3 is lossy compressed audio and is small enough for a web page. WAV is commonly uncompressed, so it keeps the recording at the cost of a much larger file. Video files are larger than still images of the same scene because they store many frames, often with sound. Choosing a format is a design decision: a club poster that will be printed at A3 size should not start life as a tiny, heavily compressed JPEG. A page that must load on school Wi-Fi should not embed an uncompressed WAV of the whole assembly.

example.scenario: The student union needs a crest on the website, a photo of the stall, and a 30-second welcome message. The crest has a transparent background. The photo is a normal camera picture.
example.walkthrough: The crest should be a PNG or a vector file so the edges stay sharp and the background can be transparent. JPEG would add blur and a solid background box. The stall photo can be a JPEG of reasonable size, because a photograph tolerates lossy compression. The welcome message can be an MP3 so the page stays small; a WAV of the same clip would be much larger. GIF would be a weak choice for the photograph because of the 256-colour limit. None of these choices changes the need for permission if the crest or the photo belongs to someone else.

traps: Using JPEG for a logo that needs a transparent background.
Saying PNG is lossy. PNG compression is lossless.
Choosing WAV for a short web audio clip when file size matters, without a reason to keep it uncompressed.

terms.definition: A lossy image format commonly used for photographs.
A lossless image format that can include transparency.
A lossy compressed audio format that keeps files smaller than uncompressed WAV.
Compression that reduces file size by permanently discarding some of the original data.

L6.2.title: File Size, Compression and Design Choices
L6.2.concept: File size decides whether a product is practical. For an uncompressed bitmap, size in bytes is width times height times colour depth in bits, divided by 8. Doubling both the width and the height multiplies the pixel count by four. Increasing colour depth from 8 bits to 24 bits multiplies the uncompressed size by three, and it raises the number of colours from 256 to about 16.7 million. Compression reduces the stored size. Lossless compression can be reversed exactly, which matters for a logo or a data file you must not damage. Lossy compression is acceptable for a photo or a podcast when the audience will not notice the lost detail. Design starts with the audience and the purpose, not with an effect. A revision page for classmates needs readable text, a clear heading, working links and a file that opens quickly. A video that auto-plays with sound can be inaccessible and annoying in a classroom. Text alternatives, captions on a video, and contrast between text and background help more users, including users who cannot see or hear the media. Export a copy at the size you will publish, and keep a master if you may need to edit again.

example.scenario: A 640 by 480 bitmap uses 24-bit colour and is uncompressed. The club wants to put it on a page that many students open at lunch on Wi-Fi.
example.walkthrough: Uncompressed size = 640 times 480 times 24, divided by 8. That is 307200 pixels times 3 bytes = 921600 bytes, about 900 KB before any other page files. That is heavy for a simple illustration. Export a smaller pixel size, or a JPEG at a sensible quality, and the download drops sharply. If the picture is a diagram with thin lines, a vector or PNG may stay clearer than a heavily compressed JPEG. State the unit. 921600 bits would be the wrong unit, because each pixel already contributes 24 bits and you then divide by 8.

traps: Forgetting to divide by 8 and giving the answer in bits.
Saying lossless compression throws away detail. Lossy compression does that; lossless does not.
Enlarging a small bitmap and expecting it to stay sharp. Bitmap enlargement shows the pixels; vector graphics do not.

terms.definition: Compression that can be reversed to restore the original data exactly.
The number of pixels in an image, often given as width times height.
Text shown with a video or audio clip so the content can be followed without the soundtrack.
The people the product is for; their devices and needs should drive format and file size.

L7.1.title: Sequence, Variables and Pseudocode
L7.1.concept: An algorithm is a finite set of steps that solves a problem. Pseudocode writes those steps in structured English so a person can follow them before anyone chooses Python or another language used in class. The compulsory programming module expects you to implement the same ideas in the language your school teaches; the exam logic is the same. A sequence runs steps from top to bottom, once each, unless a later construct says otherwise. A variable is a named place that stores a value which can change. A constant is a named value that the algorithm should not change. The arrow ← means assignment: total ← 0 stores zero in total. INPUT reads a value from the user. OUTPUT sends a result out. Only the steps that are written actually happen. Do not invent an extra calculation in a trace. Worked example: total ← 0, then total ← total + 5, then OUTPUT total. The output is 5, not 0, because the second assignment replaced the stored value. Use meaningful names. A variable called x is harder to trace than one called score.

example.scenario:
Trace this pseudocode. What is output?

sum ← 0
FOR i FROM 1 TO 3
    sum ← sum + i
END FOR
OUTPUT sum
example.walkthrough: This algorithm uses a variable sum, starting at 0, and a counter i. The loop is iteration, taught fully in the next lesson, but the trace is mechanical. When i is 1, sum becomes 1. When i is 2, sum becomes 3. When i is 3, sum becomes 6. END FOR stops the repetition. OUTPUT sum displays 6. Students who output 0 have ignored the additions. Students who output 3 have stopped after the counter, not the sum. Write a column for i and a column for sum.

traps: Adding steps that are not in the pseudocode, such as dividing by the count when the algorithm never does that.
Treating ← as a comparison. It is assignment. Comparison uses a condition such as IF score >= 50.
Saying pseudocode only works in one programming language. It is a planning notation; the school language implements it.

terms.definition: A finite sequence of steps that solves a stated problem.
A structured way of writing an algorithm so it can be read and traced before coding.
A named store whose value can change while the algorithm runs.
Storing a value in a variable, written with ← in this course.

L7.2.title: Selection and Iteration
L7.2.concept: Selection chooses a path. IF condition THEN one set of steps ELSE another set ENDIF. Only one branch runs. A condition is a comparison, such as mark >= 50. The boundary matters: if the pass mark is 50, a test of mark > 50 treats 50 as a fail, which is a logic error when 50 should pass. Nested IFs are allowed, but each IF needs its own ENDIF and you must trace the conditions in order. Iteration repeats steps. A FOR loop repeats a known number of times: FOR i FROM 1 TO 4 means i takes 1, 2, 3 and 4. A WHILE loop repeats while a condition stays true, and the steps inside must change something that can make the condition false, or the loop never ends. Example: n ← 1, WHILE n < 8, n ← n * 2, END WHILE, OUTPUT n. The values of n are 1, then 2, then 4, then 8. When n becomes 8 the condition n < 8 is false, so the loop stops and the output is 8. Count the repetitions from the trace, not from a guess.

example.scenario: A program should output "Pass" when a mark is 50 or above, and "Fail" otherwise. A student writes IF mark > 50 THEN OUTPUT "Pass" ELSE OUTPUT "Fail" ENDIF and tests it with 50.
example.walkthrough: The condition mark > 50 is false when mark is 50, so the ELSE branch runs and the output is "Fail". The requirement says 50 or above should pass, so the condition must be mark >= 50. This is a logic error: the algorithm runs, but the result is wrong on the boundary. It is not a syntax error, because the IF structure is complete. A FOR loop would be the wrong construct if the task is a single decision rather than a repetition.

traps: Using > when the specification says "or above", which includes the boundary value.
Expecting both the THEN and the ELSE branches to run. Selection runs one of them.
Writing a WHILE loop whose body never changes the condition, so it cannot stop.

terms.definition: A construct that chooses which steps to run, written with IF, THEN, ELSE and ENDIF.
A construct that repeats steps, such as FOR or WHILE.
A value at the edge of a condition, such as the lowest mark that should count as a pass.
An error in which the algorithm runs but produces the wrong result.

L7.3.title: Dry Runs, Test Data and Errors
L7.3.concept: A dry run, or trace, executes the algorithm on paper. Draw a column for each variable that changes, and a column for output. Update a cell only when that step runs. This is how you check a loop count and a total. Test data is chosen on purpose. Normal data is a typical valid value, such as a mark of 63 when marks run from 0 to 100. Boundary data sits on the edge, such as 0 and 100, and just outside if you are checking the rejection, such as -1 and 101. Abnormal or erroneous data is the wrong type or a value the algorithm should reject, such as the letter A in a mark. One test is not enough. Syntax errors break the rules of the language, so the program does not run: a missing ENDIF, or a misspelled keyword. Logic errors run and give the wrong answer, such as adding 1 too many times in a loop. Runtime errors start and then fail on some data, such as dividing by a count that is still zero. In a trace question, the marks come from the values in the table. If your output column does not match the question, the bug is in your trace, not in a feature you wish the algorithm had.

example.scenario:
Dry-run this algorithm and state the output.

count ← 0
WHILE count < 3
    count ← count + 1
END WHILE
OUTPUT count
example.walkthrough: Start with count equal to 0. The condition 0 < 3 is true, so count becomes 1. Then 1 < 3, count becomes 2. Then 2 < 3, count becomes 3. Then 3 < 3 is false, so the loop ends. OUTPUT count displays 3. A student who answers 2 stopped one repetition early. A student who answers 4 used <= by mistake. The test value 3 is the boundary where the loop must stop. Abnormal data does not appear here because the algorithm reads no input. If a later version divided a total by count before the loop, that would be a runtime error when count is still 0.

traps: Stopping the trace one step early, or using the wrong comparison at the boundary.
Calling a wrong answer a syntax error when the algorithm is structurally valid. A wrong result is a logic error.
Testing only one comfortable value, such as 50, and never testing 0, 100 or a blank input.

terms.definition: A paper execution of an algorithm, usually recorded in a trace table.
A typical valid input used to check the ordinary path.
An input on the edge of what should be accepted or rejected.
An error that breaks the rules of the language so the program cannot run.

L8.1.title: Malware, Phishing and Unauthorised Access
L8.1.concept: A threat is something that can harm data, a system or a person. Malware is software written to do harm. A virus attaches itself to a host file and spreads when that file is copied and run. A worm spreads across a network by itself and does not need to attach to a host file. A Trojan horse pretends to be useful software; it does not replicate in the way a virus does, but it can open a way in once a user installs it. Spyware collects information without a proper notice. Ransomware locks or encrypts the victim's files and demands payment. The school response is to disconnect the machine, tell a teacher or technician, and restore from a clean backup. Paying is not a recovery plan. Phishing is a fake message, often an email or a text, that tricks a person into typing a password or personal data on a lookalike page. Pharming redirects a user to a fake site even when the real address was used, often by interfering with name lookup. Unauthorised access is using a system or an account without permission. Hacking is a form of that. Describe what the threat does. Do not describe how to carry one out.

example.scenario: A classmate forwards a message that looks like the school office and asks for the portal password "to confirm the account". Another machine on the LAN has started sending copies of a program to other computers without anyone opening a file.
example.walkthrough: The message is phishing: it imitates a trusted sender to steal a password. The correct action is to ignore the link, not to reply with the password, and to tell the teacher so the school can warn others. The second case fits a worm, because it spreads across the network by itself rather than waiting inside a host file that a user opens. A Trojan would have needed someone to install a program that looked useful. A virus would be attached to a file that gets shared and run. None of these cases is solved by typing the password into the message.

traps: Calling every harmful program a virus. Worms, Trojans, spyware and ransomware are not the same.
Saying a Trojan copies itself across a network like a worm. A Trojan relies on a user installing it.
Entering a password because the message uses the school logo. Logos are easy to copy; that is phishing.

terms.definition: Malware that attaches to a host file and spreads when that file is shared and run.
Malware that spreads across a network by itself, without a host file.
Malware disguised as useful software. It does not replicate by itself.
A fake message that tricks someone into revealing a password or personal data.

L8.2.title: Passwords, Encryption, Firewalls and Backups
L8.2.concept: Protection should match the threat. A strong password is long, is not a name or a birthday, is not reused on every site, and is not shared. Two-factor authentication adds a second check, often a code from a phone or a token: something you know plus something you have. A firewall filters network traffic according to rules, blocking some connections from outside and sometimes limiting what leaves the LAN. It does not by itself find a virus already sitting in a file. Anti-malware software detects known malicious programs and needs updates, because new malware appears after the last list was made. Encryption scrambles data so that only someone with the key can read it. HTTPS encrypts the traffic between a browser and a website; it does not prove the site owner is honest. A backup is a separate copy used after data is lost or damaged. A copy on the same disk does not survive the failure of that disk. A useful school backup is stored somewhere else and is tested by restoring a file. Incremental ideas can be left at this level: a full backup copies everything; a later backup can copy what changed. No single control is enough. Ransomware defeats a password if the only backup was on the encrypted machine.

example.scenario: The school server is behind a firewall. One teacher keeps the only copy of S6 marks in a folder on that server, and also emails the spreadsheet to a personal account over a page that shows https. The teacher uses the password "teacher".
example.walkthrough: The firewall reduces unwanted connections, but it does not replace a backup. One folder on the server is a single copy: disk failure or ransomware on that server would lose the marks. A separate backup, checked by restoring a file, is the missing control. HTTPS encrypts the email connection in transit, so people on the path cannot easily read it, but the personal mailbox is another place the file can leak. The password "teacher" is short and guessable, and it should not be shared or reused. Anti-malware on the server would address malicious files; it would not make the weak password strong.

traps: Saying a firewall encrypts the contents of every file on the disk. Encryption does that job; a firewall filters traffic.
Treating HTTPS as proof that a website is trustworthy.
Keeping the only backup on the same disk as the original file.

terms.definition: Software or hardware that filters network traffic according to rules.
Scrambling data so that only a holder of the key can read it.
HTTP with encryption of the data in transit between the browser and the site.
A separate copy of data, kept so it can be restored after loss or damage.

L8.3.title: Safe and Responsible Online Behaviour
L8.3.concept: Security also depends on habits. Do not share passwords, one-time codes or identity-card numbers in a chat or a form you did not expect. Lock the screen when you leave a school computer, and sign out of a shared browser. Check the address before you type a password, and treat urgent threats in a message as a reason to slow down, not to click. Install software from a known source, because a "free game" from a random page is a common way a Trojan arrives. Public Wi-Fi can be observed by others, so a homework portal should be used over HTTPS, and banking does not belong on an open cafe network. Permissions matter: a document shared as "anyone with the link" may be wider than the class. Report bullying and suspicious messages to a teacher rather than replying. Physical safety counts too: a logged-in computer in an empty room is unauthorised access waiting to happen. These habits support the technical controls in the previous lesson. A strong password does nothing if it is written on a sticky note on the monitor. In an answer, name the habit and the harm it prevents.

example.scenario: After a group project, one member posts the shared-drive link into a public social-media story so "people can see our slides", and leaves the library computer logged into the school email.
example.walkthrough: The link permission is now far wider than the group. Anyone who opens the story may read or copy the files, including names or photos that were only meant for the class. The setting should be changed back to the project members, and a teacher should be told if personal data was exposed. The logged-in library computer lets the next person read the email. Sign out, and do not store the password in the shared browser. Neither mistake needs a hacker who breaks encryption. Both are failures of safe use. A firewall at the school does not undo a link that was deliberately made public.

traps: Posting a private sharing link on a public page and calling it safe because the file is "in the cloud".
Leaving a shared computer logged in. The next user inherits the session.
Assuming the firewall stops a user from publishing a file they are allowed to open.

terms.definition: A login that asks for a password and a second check, such as a code from a phone.
Ending a session so the next person at a shared computer cannot use the account.
A setting that decides who can view or edit a file.
A wireless network open to many people, which is a poor place to send sensitive data.

L9.1.title: Copyright, Licensing and Plagiarism
L9.1.concept: Copyright protects original work such as text, photos, music, video and program code. In Hong Kong it arises automatically; you do not register a work in order to own the copyright. Using someone else's work in a project, a website or a video needs permission, or a licence that already allows that use. Putting the school name on a copied logo does not create a new copyright. Fair dealing exists in limited situations, but it is not a blanket excuse that all schoolwork is exempt. The safe exam answer is to get permission or use material whose licence allows the use, and to say what you did. Software licences differ. Commercial software is paid for. Shareware can be tried and then must be paid for if you keep using it. Freeware costs nothing to use, but it is still copyrighted and the source code is usually not provided. Open-source software lets you read and change the source code under a licence, which may still require you to give credit or to share changes. Free of charge and open source are not the same. Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words, pictures or code as your own. Citing the source avoids plagiarism; it does not by itself clear the copyright.

example.scenario: A student pastes a pop song and a company logo into a club video, writes "I do not own this" in the description, and says freeware rules mean school projects are allowed to use anything.
example.walkthrough: The song and the logo are other people's copyright. A caption that admits copying avoids pretending the work is yours, so it helps with plagiarism, but it is not permission. The video still needs a licence or the owner's consent before it is published. Freeware is a software licence for programs the owner has released at no charge; it does not cover every song and logo. Open source would matter only if the item were released under an open-source licence, which a pop song is not. The practical fix is to use music and artwork the club has permission to use, or work the club created itself.

traps: Thinking a credit line replaces copyright permission.
Saying freeware means any file on the Internet is free to copy.
Confusing open source with "no rules". An open-source licence still sets conditions.

terms.definition: The legal right of the creator to control copying and other uses of an original work.
Software that costs nothing to use, but remains under copyright.
Software whose source code may be viewed and changed under the terms of its licence.
Presenting another person's work as your own.

L9.2.title: Personal Data, Health and the Digital Divide
L9.2.concept: Personal data identifies a living person, directly or indirectly: a name with a class, a phone number, a photograph, an identity-card number. Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance sets out six data protection principles. Collect data for a lawful purpose related to your work, and do not collect more than you need. Keep it accurate and do not keep it longer than necessary. Use it only for the original purpose, or a directly related purpose, unless the person consents or the law allows another use. Protect it from unauthorised access or accidental loss. Be open about what you collect and why. Let people ask to see their data and to correct it. A lunch survey that demands an identity-card number fails the "not excessive" idea, because a class and a menu choice would do. Emailing a parent contact list to the whole form fails security and purpose. Health risks of long computer use include eye strain, repetitive strain and backache. Reduce them with an adjustable chair, a screen at a comfortable height, space to rest the arms, and regular breaks. The digital divide is the gap in access to devices, connections and skills. Equity of access also means a page that a disabled user can operate, for example with text alternatives and captions. Indulgence in online activities can crowd out sleep and study; that is a health and social issue, not only a technical one.

example.scenario: A club signup form asks for the student's name, class, phone number and Hong Kong identity-card number, "just in case". The spreadsheet is then attached to a message sent to every member.
example.walkthrough: Name, class and a phone number may be relevant if the club needs to contact members. The identity-card number is excessive for a signup, so it should not be collected. Sending the whole spreadsheet to every member lets people see one another's numbers, which is a security failure and a use beyond "the committee contacts you". Access should be limited to the people who need it, and the file should be deleted when the signup is over, rather than kept forever. A health point is separate: if students build the form in one long sitting, breaks and seating still matter. A scanned identity card on a public page would be a worse exposure of the same data.

traps: Collecting an identity-card number because it is easy, when the purpose does not need it.
Sending a contact list to everyone on the list.
Saying the digital divide only means some people own a more expensive phone. It includes connectivity, skills and accessible design.

terms.definition: Data that identifies a living person, such as a name, a photo or an identity-card number.
The six principles in Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance on collection, accuracy, use, security, openness, and access.
Unequal access to digital devices, connectivity or skills.
Arranging the workplace, including chair, screen and breaks, to reduce physical strain.

L10.1.title: How the ICT Exam Is Set Out
L10.1.concept: HKDSE ICT has a public examination and a school-based assessment. On the assessment framework published for recent years, Paper 1 is the compulsory part, lasting 2 hours and carrying 55 percent of the subject. Section A is multiple-choice and Section B is short and structured questions; everyone answers both. Paper 2 lasts 1 hour 30 minutes, carries 25 percent, and asks you to answer all the questions in any two electives: Databases, Web Application Development, and Algorithm and Programming. School-based assessment carries 20 percent and, in the current handbook, is two guided tasks: design and implementation, then testing and evaluation. These weightings are a summary of the published framework, not a promise that a future handbook will never change. Before you revise the timing, open the framework for the year you sit. Command words tell you the shape of the answer. State, name or identify wants a short fact. Describe wants the main features. Explain wants a reason, often with "because". Suggest wants a practical idea that fits the case given, not a definition copied from notes. Compare needs both sides. Outline wants the main points in brief. Marks are lost by writing a paragraph when the question says "state", and by stating a term when the question says "explain".

example.scenario: A 2-mark question says "State two advantages of a star topology over a bus." A student writes a page about how fibre works.
example.walkthrough: "State" wants two short advantages, for example: a fault in one cable affects only one device, and it is easier to add a device by connecting it to the central switch. Fibre is a transmission medium, not a topology, so that page does not answer the question. Two marks means two points, not two paragraphs. If the question had said "explain", each point would need a because. If it had said "suggest" for a particular school, the answer would have to use the case, such as separate buildings or a shared server. Check the elective: a databases technique will not score on a Paper 2 option you did not choose.

traps: Ignoring the command word and writing everything you know about the topic.
Revising all three Paper 2 electives in the exam room. You answer the two your school entered.
Memorising a weighting from a friend's notes for a different exam year without checking the framework.

terms.definition: The verb in a question, such as state or explain, that tells you the form of the answer.
The compulsory paper: multiple-choice plus short and structured questions.
The elective paper: all the questions in two of the three options.
Teacher-assessed guided tasks that form part of the subject mark.

L10.2.title: Answering the Common ICT Question Types
L10.2.concept: Three question types carry most of the paper. System and network questions want the right device or idea for the case, plus a reason. Name a switch for a room full of computers, and say that it forwards traffic inside the LAN. Do not say "use a better computer". Database questions want keys, validation and the difference between a form and a report. If a field can repeat, it is not a primary key. If a check only tests the range, say clearly that a wrong but in-range value still passes. Algorithm questions want a trace or a short piece of pseudocode that matches the words of the question. Use a column for every variable that changes. Do not add a step the algorithm does not contain. Calculations want working and a unit. Bitmap size is width times height times colour depth, divided by 8 for bytes. If you forget the division, label the result as bits only when that is what you actually computed. The traps that return every year are: Internet versus World Wide Web, validation versus verification, virus versus worm, freeware versus open source, RAM versus secondary storage, and a credit line versus copyright permission. Finish by reading the question stem once more and checking that every mark point is a point the stem asked for.

example.scenario:
A question shows this pseudocode and asks for the output only.

mark ← 50
IF mark > 50 THEN
    OUTPUT "Pass"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Fail"
ENDIF
example.walkthrough: The output is Fail. The condition is greater than 50, and 50 is not greater than 50, so the ELSE branch runs. An answer of Pass repeats the everyday meaning of a pass mark and ignores the symbol in the algorithm. Writing a paragraph about boundary testing may earn nothing if the command is to state the output. In a 3-mark "explain" version, you would add that 50 fails the strict greater-than test, so the condition does not match a rule of 50 or above. Units, keys and command words are the same habit: answer the question that was set.

traps: Tracing what you think the program should do, instead of the condition that is written.
Giving a file size with no unit, or in bits when the question says bytes.
Explaining a term the question did not ask for, and skipping the case in the stem.

terms.definition: A table of variable values and outputs used to dry-run an algorithm.
One fact or reason that earns a mark. Match the number of points to the marks.
The calculation steps shown before the final number, including the unit.
The situation printed before the question. Use its facts in a suggest or explain answer.

L1.4.title: The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle and Cache
L1.4.concept: The CPU does not run a whole program in one jump. It repeats a fetch-decode-execute cycle. Fetch means the control unit reads the next instruction from memory. Decode means it works out what that instruction is asking for, such as an addition or a comparison. Execute means the right part carries it out. An addition is done by the arithmetic and logic unit. A store instruction writes a result back to memory. Then the cycle starts again with the next instruction. Main memory is large enough for the program, but it is slower than the CPU. Cache is a small, fast store beside the CPU that keeps copies of instructions or data just used, because the same ones are often needed again. A cache hit avoids a slower trip to RAM. A cache miss means the copy was not there, so it is fetched from RAM. Cache is not a backup of the user's files and it does not replace an SSD. If the power goes off, RAM and cache do not keep the attendance file. That file still belongs in secondary storage. Name the stage or the store. Do not describe how a chip is manufactured.

example.scenario: A quiz program adds two scores that are already in RAM, then writes the total into the pupil's file on the SSD. The same two scores are used again a moment later.
example.walkthrough: Fetching the add instruction, decoding it, and executing it in the ALU is one cycle. The scores may be copied into cache because they are used again, which is a hit the second time. The total in RAM would vanish at shutdown, so writing the file is secondary storage, not a cache job. Calling the SSD a cache, or saying the ALU fetches the instruction, mixes up the parts.

traps: Saying cache keeps the only copy of a file after shutdown.
Giving the ALU the job of fetching the next instruction. Fetching is directed by the control unit.
Treating two cores as a promise that every program finishes in half the time.

terms.definition: The repeating cycle in which the CPU reads an instruction, works out what it means, and carries it out.
A small, fast store that keeps copies of recently used instructions or data close to the CPU.
The needed copy is already in cache, so the CPU does not have to read it from slower main memory.
A processing unit inside the CPU. Extra cores can run suitable work at the same time.

L2.4.title: Converting Bases and Spotting Overflow
L2.4.concept: Binary, denary and hexadecimal are three ways to write the same whole number. Convert by place value, not by guessing the length of the string. In binary the places from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and so on. The binary number 101101 is 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45. Hexadecimal groups four bits into one digit. The digits 0 to 9 keep their usual meaning, and A to F mean 10 to 15. The hex number A3 is 10 × 16 + 3 = 163. Two hex digits are one byte. An unsigned 8-bit integer can hold 0 to 255. If a sum such as 250 + 10 equals 260, it does not fit, and that is overflow. Text has its own size rule. In the ASCII model used in this course, one character is one byte, so the four letters NOTE use 4 bytes, which is 32 bits. Do not call 32 bits 32 bytes. Show the place values in the working. A bare final number with no unit, or a hex digit read as a denary digit, drops the mark even when the idea was right.

example.scenario: Convert binary 101101 to denary, convert hex A3 to denary, and decide whether 250 + 10 fits in an 8-bit unsigned integer.
example.walkthrough: 101101 uses the places 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. The 1-bits contribute 32, 8, 4 and 1, so the denary value is 45. A is 10, so A3 is 160 + 3 = 163. 250 + 10 = 260. The largest 8-bit unsigned value is 255, so 260 overflows. A student who reads A as 1 gets 19, and a student who says 260 fits has forgotten the top of the range.

traps: Reading the hex digit A as the denary digit 1.
Calling an overflow result valid because the sum is still a whole number.
Mixing bits and bytes: 8 bits are 1 byte, so 32 bits are 4 bytes.

terms.definition: The value of a digit based on its position, such as 32 for the leftmost bit of 101101.
A result that is outside the range the chosen representation can store.
Eight bits. In this course one ASCII character uses one byte.
Base 16. Digits run from 0 to 9 and then A to F.

L3.3.title: Bandwidth, Delay and Addresses on a School Network
L3.3.concept: A network is not judged by one number. Bandwidth is how much data the link can carry in a given time. Latency is how long you wait before the first response arrives. A link can have room for a large file and still feel slow if every request is delayed. Inside one room, a switch forwards frames to the computer that should receive them. A hub is cruder: it repeats traffic to every port. A router joins different networks. An address that begins 192.168 is, in this course, a typical private address used on the LAN. It is not the public address of a website, and it does not mean the computer has no network card. The SSID is the name of a Wi-Fi network. The password is a separate secret. A fixed lab computer often uses a cable because that link is not shared with every phone in the corridor and is less affected by walls. One cable does not turn a computer into a WAN. When a question says suggest, name the device or the medium and give the reason that matches the room in the stem.

example.scenario: Thirty desktop computers in one lab share a file server. The PCs do not move. Users say the Wi-Fi feels slow at lunchtime when phones join the same name.
example.walkthrough: The lab is a LAN. Desktops that stay on one desk can use cables to a switch, so they are not fighting the phones for the wireless channel. The SSID is only the name those phones select. The server is reached inside the school network. Traffic to a different network, such as a website, goes through a router. Saying the switch creates a WAN, or that the SSID is the password, does not answer the case.

traps: Treating bandwidth and latency as the same word.
Calling the SSID the password.
Using a router when the traffic never leaves the LAN, or a switch when it must.

terms.definition: How much data a link can carry in a given time.
The delay before data starts to arrive.
The name of a wireless network.
An address used inside a local network, such as one beginning 192.168 in this course.

L6.3.title: Choosing a Format from the Numbers
L6.3.concept: A format is a decision about quality, size and what the file is for. MIDI stores instructions for notes, instruments and timing, so a tune can be small, but it is not a recording of a voice. WAV stores sampled sound and is often uncompressed, so it is large and keeps the recording. A bit rate such as 128 kbps means about 128 kilobits of audio data for each second. It is not a pixel width. Pictures follow the bitmap rule. An uncompressed frame of 100 by 50 pixels at 8-bit colour is 100 × 50 × 8 = 40 000 bits, which is 5 000 bytes. Ten such frames, with no sound, are 50 000 bytes. JPEG is a poor choice when the logo needs a transparent background. A storyboard is not a codec. It is a plan of shots and order, drawn before filming, so a missing scene is noticed while the event can still be filmed. Start from the job: voice recording, logo, or a timed clip. Then compute a size if the question gives width, height, depth or a frame count, and label the unit.

example.scenario: The club needs a transparent crest, a 10-frame animation of 100 by 50 pixels at 8-bit colour with no sound, and a piano part that is not a recording of someone playing.
example.walkthrough: PNG keeps transparency, so it fits the crest better than JPEG. The animation is 5 000 bytes per frame and 50 000 bytes for ten frames, before any player overhead the question did not mention. The piano part can be MIDI because it stores note instructions rather than a waveform. A student who answers 40 000 bytes has left the size in bits for one frame, or has forgotten to multiply by ten.

traps: Leaving a bitmap size in bits when the question asks for bytes.
Using JPEG for a logo that must keep a transparent background.
Describing MIDI as a sampled recording of speech.

terms.definition: How much audio data is used for each second of playback, such as 128 kbps.
A format that stores musical instructions rather than a sampled waveform.
A planned sequence of shots, drawn before filming.
One still image in a video or animation. Uncompressed size is the bitmap size times the number of frames.

L9.3.title: Collect Only What the Task Needs
L9.3.concept: Social and ethical questions in this course are about a decision in a school case, not about a statute number. Copyright still applies when you name the source. Attribution tells the reader where a chart came from. Permission, or a licence that allows the use, is what lets you copy it onto a public page. Personal data should match the task. A lunch poll needs the meal choice. It does not need an identity-card number, a home address or a parent's salary. Collecting more is not fairer. It creates copies that can be leaked or kept too long. After the signup is finished, data that is no longer needed should not sit in a shared inbox. Access matters in the same way. An assembly video with no captions and no transcript leaves out pupils who cannot follow the soundtrack. Health is part of the same responsible use. A screen near eye level, a supported back, and short breaks reduce strain. A dark room and an hour with no pause do not. In an explain answer, name the principle and tie it to the fact in the stem. A definition with no link to the case is thin.

example.scenario: The class committee wants a lunch poll. The form asks for HKID number, home address, parent's salary and the meal. They plan to post a copied news chart, with the site name written under it, on the public page that announces the result.
example.walkthrough: Keep the meal choice. Drop the identity number, address and salary because the poll does not use them. Naming the news site is attribution, not permission, so the chart should not go on the public page unless the club has a right to use it. An answer that says more data is always safer, or that a caption replaces copyright, misses both decisions.

traps: Treating attribution as a substitute for permission.
Collecting an identity number because the form looks more official.
Assuming a video is accessible because it can be played.

terms.definition: Naming the source of a work. It is not the same as permission to copy it.
Collecting only the personal data the task actually needs.
On-screen text of the spoken words, used so more pupils can follow a video.
Arranging the workstation and the breaks so long computer use causes less strain.

L10.3.title: A Worked File-Size Answer and the Command Word
L10.3.concept: Marks follow the command word and the working. Compare means both things in the question: what they share and how they differ. State means the result, not a paragraph of definitions. Explain means the result plus the reason. A file-size question that asks for bytes needs the unit in the final line. For an uncompressed bitmap, multiply width by height by the colour depth in bits, then divide by 8. A 200 by 100 image at 24-bit colour is 200 × 100 × 24 = 480 000 bits = 60 000 bytes. Writing 480 000 alone answers a different question. Paper structure is part of the same habit. Paper 1 is the compulsory paper. Paper 2 is the two electives the school entered. Answering a third elective, or skipping Paper 1, does not match the entry. For a trace, the output is whatever the printed steps produce. If the command is state the output, give that output. A preferred algorithm you were not asked to write earns nothing. Check the stem once more: every mark point should be something the question requested.

example.scenario: A question says: "A bitmap is 200 pixels by 100 pixels with a colour depth of 24 bits. State its uncompressed size in bytes." It is worth 2 marks.
example.walkthrough: The working is 200 × 100 × 24 = 480 000 bits. Divide by 8 to get 60 000 bytes. The final line should say 60 000 bytes. One mark is often the method and one is the answer with the unit. 480 000 bytes is the common slip. A paragraph about JPEG compression does not answer state, because the question said uncompressed and asked for the size.

traps: Stopping at the bit count when the question says bytes.
Answering all three Paper 2 electives, or only one side of a compare.
Replacing a stated output with a definition of the keyword OUTPUT.

terms.definition: Give similarities and differences for both items named in the question.
Give the required fact or result without a long extra explanation.
The calculation steps shown before the final number, including the unit.
The two Paper 2 options the school entered for that candidate.
